strengths: Introduces a large-scale (1M+) and diverse MER training dataset (UniMER-1M) spanning simple printed, complex printed, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions, substantially larger and more varied than prior datasets like IM2LATEX-100K and Pix2tex.

Proposes UniMER-Test, a well-structured benchmark with four distinct evaluation dimensions (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE) that better reflects real-world MER challenges than existing benchmarks focused mainly on simple printed or handwritten expressions.
The Length-Aware Module is a reasonable and lightweight architectural addition, with an ablation (Table 4) showing consistent gains especially on complex/long expressions (CPE).

Extensive experiments including ablations on data composition, augmentation, and LAM, plus comparisons against both printed-formula SOTA (Pix2tex, Texify) and handwritten-formula SOTA (CAN, SAN, CoMER, etc.) on standard CROHME/HME100K benchmarks, showing consistent improvements.
Data augmentation strategy (weather noise, dilation/erosion, etc.) is shown empirically to meaningfully help on noisy/screen-captured data (SCE), addressing a practically important robustness gap.
The dataset and benchmark, if released as claimed, could be a genuinely useful community resource given the scarcity of diverse, large-scale MER data.
weaknesses: Technical description of the Length-Aware Module is vague: it is unclear how length is discretized/represented (is it a classification over C length bins, or a regression?), how ground-truth length labels are obtained/binned, and how the length embedding is combined with token/position embeddings (concatenation vs. addition) — insufficient detail for reproducibility.

The performance gain from LAM alone is quite small and only clearly beneficial on CPE (+2% BLEU), with negligible or slightly negative effects on other subsets (Table 4), raising questions about how much the module truly contributes versus data/augmentation, which appear to be the dominant factors.

Dataset construction methodology lacks critical detail: for SCE, only 4,744 test formulas were manually collected/verified via Mathpix + human correction (no SCE training data appears to be described distinctly, raising concerns about train/test distribution match for this subset); details about de-duplication and any train/test leakage checks (e.g., overlap between web/Arxiv sourced formulas in UniMER-1M and existing test sets) are not provided.

No statistical significance testing or repeated runs are reported; single-run results are used for all comparisons and ablations, which is a common but limiting practice given some improvements are marginal (e.g., LAM contribution).

Comparisons with LVLM-based approaches (Nougat, Vary) are only qualitative (Fig. 5, three samples) rather than quantitative on the full UniMER-Test benchmark, weakening the claim that they are only outperformed by UniMERNet.

The writing has some clarity issues and minor grammatical errors, and cross-references between sections/tables occasionally lack precision (e.g., exact number of SCE training samples used is not explicitly stated).

Novelty of the core architectural contribution (LAM: self-attention + global pooling + length regression fed as embedding) is incremental relative to existing counting/length-aware modules such as CAN's counting module, and the paper's justification for why it is more suitable for LaTeX (vs. CAN's symbol counting) is somewhat hand-wavy rather than empirically isolated.
The dataset and code availability is only promised ('available at') with no working link provided in the reviewed manuscript, limiting reproducibility assessment at this stage.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale, diverse MER training dataset (UniMER-1M, ~1M samples) that substantially exceeds prior open datasets in scale and formula-length diversity, addressing a real gap in existing benchmarks that focus mainly on simple printed or handwritten expressions.

Proposes UniMER-Test, a well-structured four-way benchmark (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE) that enables fine-grained, real-world-relevant evaluation of MER robustness across formula complexity, noise, and handwriting styles -- a genuinely useful community resource.

The Length-Aware Module is a simple, well-motivated architectural addition, and its benefit is empirically isolated via ablation (Table 4), showing consistent gains particularly on complex/long formulas (CPE).

Extensive experiments span comparisons against printed-formula specialists (Pix2tex, Texify), handwritten-formula SOTA methods (CAN, SAN, CoMER, etc.), and qualitative failure-case analysis against LVLM-based approaches (Nougat), providing a fairly comprehensive validation across scenario types.

Ablations cleanly decompose the contribution of data scale/diversity, image augmentation, and LAM, allowing readers to attribute performance gains to each component rather than treating the system as a monolithic black box.
Dataset and model release (data/code availability stated) supports reproducibility and community adoption.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core architecture is a standard Swin+mBART encoder-decoder (borrowed from Donut), and the Length-Aware Module is a relatively simple auxiliary length-regression head with modest reported gains (e.g., +2% BLEU on CPE, negligible/mixed on other subsets in Table 4); the primary contribution is arguably the dataset rather than the modeling innovation.

Data collection methodology has limited transparency: the regularization/augmentation pipeline for expanding SPE/CPE via Arxiv/Wikipedia/StackExchange is described only briefly, with no analysis of potential duplicate/near-duplicate leakage between train and test splits, LaTeX rendering diversity (fonts/styles), or quality control beyond 'uncompilable expressions discarded.'

SCE test set construction relies on Mathpix-generated pseudo-labels with only two annotators for manual correction and cross-verification; annotation agreement/quality metrics are not reported, raising concerns about label reliability for this crucial 'real-world noisy' subset where performance gaps are largest.

No statistical significance testing or variance across runs is reported for any of the comparison tables, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements (especially smaller ones, e.g., LAM ablation) are robust versus noise.

The comparison with LVLM-based methods (Nougat, Vary) is only qualitative (three cherry-picked examples in Fig. 5) rather than quantitative on the full UniMER-Test benchmark, weakening the claim that these methods are decisively inferior.

The paper does not discuss computational cost/inference speed trade-offs of adding the LAM and heavier data augmentation, nor model size comparisons with baselines, limiting assessment of practical deployment trade-offs.

Limited discussion of failure modes or error analysis for UniMERNet itself; the paper mostly showcases wins in Fig. 5 without deeper analysis of remaining error categories (e.g., very long formulas, specific symbol confusions).

strengths: Introduces a large-scale (1M+ sample) MER training dataset (UniMER-1M) that is substantially larger and more diverse than prior datasets like IM2LATEX-100K and Pix2tex, spanning simple, complex, screen-captured, and handwritten formulas.
Proposes UniMER-Test, a well-constructed and diverse benchmark (SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE) that better reflects real-world MER challenges than existing narrow benchmarks, addressing a genuine gap in the field.

The architectural modifications (Fine-Grained Embedding, ConvEnhance, Removal of Shift Window, Squeeze Attention) are simple, well-motivated, and empirically validated via systematic ablations (Tables 2, 3, 6-9), showing consistent accuracy and speed improvements over a Texify/Swin/mBART baseline.

Extensive experiments, including comparisons with SOTA (Pix2tex, Texify, Nougat), pretraining ablations, and depth/architecture sensitivity studies, provide reasonably thorough empirical support for the claims.

The dataset construction pipeline (deduplication via perceptual hashing, LaTeX normalization, balanced length sampling, diverse rendering fonts/DPIs, data augmentation strategy) is described in good technical detail, aiding reproducibility.
Practical utility: the resulting model and dataset appear directly useful for real-world document/formula extraction pipelines, and the paper reports plans for public release of data/models/code.
weaknesses: Novelty of the architectural contributions is incremental: FGE, ConvEnhance, and Squeeze Attention are relatively straightforward adaptations of existing ideas (overlapping conv patch embedding, depthwise conv enhancement, low-rank/bottleneck attention) already explored in the vision transformer literature; the core contribution is largely the dataset rather than fundamentally new modeling insight.

SCE test set is quite small (4,744 samples) and was annotated/corrected by only two annotators with Mathpix-assisted labeling, raising potential concerns about annotation quality, bias, and statistical robustness of results on this most 'real-world' subset.

The comparison with Nougat is potentially unfair/awkward — the paper notes it had to synthetically embed formulas in random text to accommodate Nougat's page-level design, which may not reflect Nougat's true intended use case, weakening the validity of that qualitative comparison.

Reported BLEU improvements on some subsets (e.g., SPE) are marginal (0.9%), and the paper does not report statistical significance or variance across multiple runs, making it hard to assess whether gains are robust or within noise.

Limited discussion of failure cases or error analysis beyond three cherry-picked qualitative examples (Figure 5); no quantitative breakdown of error types (e.g., symbol confusion vs. structural errors) that would substantiate claims about the encoder's fine-grained/local advantages.

The 16M image-text pretraining corpus and additional 4M LaTeX source expansion data are not released or fully specified in terms of licensing/filtering, raising some reproducibility concerns for the pretraining stage results (Table 6).

The paper's claim of 'first study on MER targeting complex real-world scenarios' is a strong claim that somewhat overlooks related large-scale document understanding efforts (e.g., Nougat, Vary) which also address real-world document/formula extraction, even if not MER-specialized; the framing could be more measured.
Some presentation issues: inconsistent test set sizes between Table 1 (23,757) and text (23,789), and dataset/table formatting typos, slightly undermining polish and clarity.
